query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (3–5 at.%) of vanadium to the equal-atomic NbMoTaW BCC alloy will reduce the dislocation core (Peierls) barrier at room temperature, thereby improving ductility without compromising high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Introduce 3–5 at.% vanadium into the NbMoTaW alloy
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature and 1600 °C, as well as standardized ion irradiation exposure assessments
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the single-phase BCC microstructure with slight electronic structure modifications
generation.mechanism: The addition of vanadium is expected to alter the near-Fermi electronic structure, thereby reducing the dislocation (Peierls) barrier and activating additional slip systems at room temperature, while the low concentration preserves the high-temperature mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance of the BCC matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, the vanadium-doped alloy should exhibit enhanced room-temperature ductility (increased elongation and lower yield strength related to easier dislocation motion), while maintaining similar high-temperature mechanical performance at 1600 °C and comparable irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy without vanadium addition
generation.boundary: The vanadium content must remain within 3–5 at.% to avoid formation of secondary phases that could destabilize the BCC structure or adversely affect high-temperature performance and irradiation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in room-temperature ductility and the precise impact on high-temperature and irradiation behavior remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of NbMoTaW alloys with vanadium additions of 0, 3, 4, and 5 at.%. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility (elongation to failure and yield strength), high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests (tensile or compressive properties), and standardized ion irradiation tests to assess microstructural stability and irradiation-induced defect density.
measurements: Room temperature elongation and yield strength
Post-irradiation hardness, defect density, and microstructure observations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, or if it exhibits a significant degradation (>predefined threshold) in high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

frame.understanding: Hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition—such as 3–5 at.% vanadium—could modify the electronic structure near the Fermi level, thereby reducing the dislocation core (Peierls) barrier at room temperature. This adjustment is expected to activate more slip systems and facilitate easier dislocation motion, enhancing ductility at room temperature. The low concentration should preserve the BCC single-phase stability, ensuring that high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance remain unaffected. Supporting evidence includes studies on similar refractory alloys where microalloying (e.g., with V or other ductility-promoting elements) has led to improved room-temperature ductility without detrimentally affecting high-temperature behavior. A falsification experiment would involve fabricating NbMoTaW alloys with 3–5 at.% V, then subjecting them to comparative mechanical testing at room temperature and 1600 °C as well as standardized ion irradiation tests to determine if the ductility improvement occurs without losses in high-temperature strength or irradiation performance relative to the untreated baseline.
